summary: Describes the NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol for signaling Quality of Service reservations. Together with GIST it gives RSVP-like function, independent of the QoS model, without multicast support. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: QoS NSLP carries requests for special network treatment from one network node to the next. Each node decides locally whether it can provide the requested service.

subtitle: How NSIS nodes signal requests for quality-of-service resources along a data path.

tldr.problem: Some traffic needs specific network treatment, but the network must know about a request before it can reserve resources along the path.
tldr.mechanism: QoS NSLP sends peer-to-peer messages between QoS nodes. A local Resource Management Function interprets the requested QoS and decides whether to configure resources.
tldr.outcome: The protocol supports sender- and receiver-initiated reservations but not multicast flows. RFC 5974 is Experimental.

today: RFC 5974 is an Experimental Protocol specification. It describes QoS signaling in the NSIS framework and does not define a particular resource-management model.

sections.title: The Role of QoS NSLP
sections.content:
The Quality of Service NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (QoS NSLP) establishes and maintains state at nodes along a data flow. That state lets network nodes arrange forwarding resources for the flow. QoS NSLP is part of the NSIS signaling framework and relies on GIST to deliver its messages.

The protocol separates signaling from resource management. QoS NSLP describes how nodes exchange requests. A local Resource Management Function handles the requested resources, and a policy function may decide whether the requester is authorized. The RFC does not define support for IP multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: QoS NSLP carries resource requests along a data path. GIST delivers the messages, while each node's local functions decide what to do with them.

sections.title: Four Message Types
sections.content:
RESERVE creates, refreshes, changes, or removes reservation state. Repeating the same RESERVE has the same effect as receiving it once. QUERY asks for information about the path without changing a reservation.

RESPONSE reports the result of a request, including an error or confirmation. NOTIFY sends information asynchronously, such as notice that state was removed or a reservation was preempted. Messages travel between neighboring QoS NSLP nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: RESERVE changes reservation state, while QUERY asks about the path without changing it. RESPONSE gives a result, and NOTIFY reports an event.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Initiation
sections.content:
In a sender-initiated reservation, the request travels in the same direction as the data flow. The first node requesting the reservation is the QNI, and the final node receiving the request is the QNR. A response can travel back along the signaling path to confirm the result.

In a receiver-initiated reservation, the reservation request travels opposite to the data flow. The receiver is responsible for requesting and maintaining the resources. The protocol also supports bidirectional reservations by binding separate signaling sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can request resources in the direction its data will travel. A receiver can instead take responsibility and send the reservation request in the opposite direction.

sections.title: QoS Models and Resource Decisions
sections.content:
A QSPEC object describes the requested resources and is interpreted by the Resource Management Function for the local QoS model. QoS NSLP treats this object as opaque. Different networks can therefore use different QoS models without changing the signaling protocol.

At each node, policy control can check authorization, and admission control can determine whether enough resources are available. If the checks succeed, the node can configure traffic classification and packet scheduling. The RFC leaves the Resource Management Function's exact behavior to the chosen QoS model.
sections.plainLanguage: QoS NSLP carries a description of the requested service but does not decide how to provide it. Each node checks permission and available resources using its own QoS model.

sections.title: Soft State and Reservation Refreshes
sections.content:
Reservation state is soft state: a node keeps it valid for a period specified by a refresh-period object. To keep the reservation, signaling must refresh the state before its lifetime ends. This lets state expire if refresh messages stop arriving.

QoS NSLP can reduce signaling overhead by refreshing an existing reservation using its session identifier and reservation sequence number, instead of repeating the full QSPEC. It also defines summary refreshes and summary teardown messages for handling multiple sessions together.
sections.plainLanguage: A reservation lasts only while nodes continue to refresh its state. A refresh can refer to an existing reservation instead of repeating all its details.
